title: How to start selling on Amazon Japan in 2026: the complete beginner's guide
description: Sell on Amazon.co.jp in 2026: ¥4,900 plan, April 2026 fee changes, 10% consumption tax and invoices, IOR/ACP, PSE and Giteki, and a 90-day launch plan.
tldr: Amazon's Japan segment had about $30.7 billion in 2025 net sales, up about 12% [s40]; only about 9.8% of Japanese retail goods sales are online, so there is room to grow [s38].
Large-volume plan: ¥4,900/month before tax; small-volume: ¥100 per item sold. Choose large-volume to run ads [s1][s2].
From 1 April 2026, referral fees rose 0.4 points on items over ¥750 (most rates are now 8.4%, 10.4% or 15.4%), while standard FBA fees for 20–80 cm items fell about ¥38 on average [s1][s3].
Example: a ¥3,000 home and kitchen item pays about ¥462 referral fee (15.4%, plus 10% tax on the fee) + ¥318 FBA = about 28% of price [s1].
Consumption tax is 10% (8% reduced rate for food) [s13]; businesses with base-period sales of ¥10 million or less are exempt unless they register for the qualified invoice system [s12].
Overseas sellers: Amazon won't be your importer of record; non-residents need an Attorney for Customs Procedures in Japan [s19][s22].
Since 25 December 2025, overseas sellers of PSE/PSC products must appoint a responsible person in Japan [s24]; wireless goods need Giteki certification [s28].
From 1 April 2028: designated large platforms become liable for consumption tax on goods foreign sellers sell through them [s46].

blocks.p: Japan is one of Amazon's biggest markets outside the US. In its 2025 annual report, Amazon put Japan segment net sales at about **$30.7 billion**, up roughly 12% from about $27.4 billion in 2024 [s40]. That figure covers Amazon's own retail sales plus seller fees and other revenue, so it is not the same as the total value of goods sold on Amazon.co.jp, but it shows the market is large and still growing.

The wider market is also growing, but slowly. Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) published its official survey on 21 October 2026: consumer e-commerce in Japan reached about **¥27.6 trillion in 2025**, up 5.5% [s38]. Physical goods sold online (the part that matters for Amazon sellers) were about **¥15.8 trillion**, up about 4%, and only about **9.8%** of all retail goods sales happened online, almost unchanged from the year before [s38][s39]. Online shopping still has room to grow, and buyers stick to a few big platforms (Amazon, Rakuten and Yahoo! Shopping).

blocks.h3: How many sellers, and how much competition?

blocks.p: Amazon does not publish an exact seller count for Japan every year. Its 2022 impact report said about **150,000 Japanese businesses** sold on Amazon, most of them small and medium-sized companies [s41]. On top of that, many overseas sellers (especially from China) list on Amazon.co.jp. Competition is highest in cheap electronics accessories, phone cases, small kitchen gadgets and generic home goods. It is lower where Japanese-language content, local certification (PSE, Giteki) or careful packaging is a barrier.

blocks.h3: AI shopping: Rufus, now 'Alexa for Shopping'

blocks.p: Amazon's AI shopping assistant **Rufus** launched in Japan as a beta for some app users in November 2024 [s30] and became available to all customers in Japan on 2 September 2025, in the app and on desktop [s29]. In May 2026 Amazon renamed Rufus to **Alexa for Shopping** in the US [s32], and Japanese media reported the same rename for Japan on 12 November 2026 [s31]. Rufus technology still powers parts of the experience behind the scenes [s32]. Shoppers ask questions and get AI answers built from your listing, images and reviews, so listings that answer real questions in natural Japanese win.

blocks.h3: What this means for a beginner

ul: **It is a big, rich, quality-sensitive market.** Japanese shoppers read reviews closely, expect perfect packaging and punish sloppy Japanese text.

**Barriers are real but learnable.** Japanese language, consumption tax, importer rules for overseas sellers and product-safety marks (PSE, PSC, Giteki) are the main hurdles. Each one is covered below.
**Fees changed in April 2026.** Referral fees went up a little on most items and standard-size FBA fees went down a little [s3]. Your margin maths must use 2026 numbers.
**Big new rules for overseas sellers are coming.** Product-safety law changes took effect on 25 December 2025 [s24], and consumption-tax 'platform taxation' for goods starts in April 2028 [s46].

callout.title: Beginner takeaway
callout.text: Japan rewards sellers who do the boring things well: correct certification, natural Japanese listings, careful packaging and fast replies. If you are willing to do that, competition is softer than on Amazon.com in many niches.

sections.title: What changed in 2025–2026 (and what is coming)

blocks.p: These are the changes a beginner on Amazon.co.jp must know about. Fee details come from Amazon's own Seller Central announcements where possible; always check the current fee page before you price.

Amended Consumer Product Safety Act and Electrical Appliances and Materials Safety Act (and two LP-gas laws) took effect. Overseas businesses selling directly to Japanese consumers, for example through a marketplace, are now clearly covered and must appoint a person in Japan responsible for safety (often called a domestic administrator) [s24][s25].
If you are based outside Japan and sell PSE or PSC products, you need a Japanese domestic administrator and must meet the notification duties yourself.

Referral fees rose 0.4 percentage points in every fee category for items whose total sale price is above ¥750 (for example 8% became 8.4%). Items at ¥750 or below kept the 5% rate and ¥30 minimum. Media, Amazon device accessories and video games went up 0.4 points regardless of price [s1][s3].
Re-run your margin maths. A ¥3,000 item pays about ¥12 more in referral fee.
FBA fulfilment fees for standard-size items measuring 20–80 cm and up to 5 kg fell by an average of ¥38 per unit, according to Amazon's notice [s3].
Mid-size standard items got slightly cheaper to fulfil. Check your tier in the current fee table [s1].
A long-term storage surcharge applies to stock stored more than 365 days [s1]; Amazon's 2026 notice is reported to set a minimum of ¥20 per unit per month [s3].
Check the exact rate in Seller Central, then remove or liquidate slow stock before it reaches a year.

From 1 October 2027, sellers of low-value goods (¥10,000 or less) shipped from abroad can apply to register as 'specified low-value asset sellers' [s46].
Watch for Amazon and National Tax Agency notices in 2027.

Platform taxation for goods: platforms designated by the National Tax Agency (over ¥5 billion a year of qualifying sales) become liable for consumption tax on goods foreign sellers sell in Japan through them. Mail-order sales of items of ¥10,000 or less shipped from abroad also become taxable sales in Japan [s46].
If you are an overseas seller, Amazon is likely to file and pay consumption tax on your sales from 2028. Until then, you are responsible yourself.
table.note: Current rates are on Amazon's pricing page [s1]; details of each change are in Amazon's Seller Central notices [s3][s4]. The 2028 tax changes are from the National Tax Agency's April 2026 notice [s46].

callout.title: Biggest 2026 change for overseas sellers
callout.text: The December 2025 product-safety amendment means Amazon and METI now expect overseas sellers of electrical goods and other regulated products to have a responsible person in Japan [s24]. Sort this out before you list, not after a listing gets removed.

sections.title: Is Amazon Japan right for you?

blocks.h3: Japan is a good first or second market if you:

ul: Live in Japan, or can work with a Japanese partner who can handle customer messages and returns.
Have a product that benefits from quality, design or a trusted brand.
Can get listings written by a native Japanese speaker, not machine translation alone.
Already sell in the US or Europe and want a third large market with different competition.
Want the fastest possible start with no language or compliance work.
Plan to sell cheap electrical or Bluetooth products without PSE or Giteki certification. These get removed and can be reported to regulators [s24][s26].
Cannot pay import consumption tax and duty upfront when your goods arrive in Japan.

blocks.h3: Selling from outside Japan (India, China, US, Europe and others)

blocks.p: Overseas sellers can register on Amazon.co.jp, but three Japan-specific problems trip almost everyone up:

ol: **Importer of Record (IOR).** Someone must be the legal importer of your goods into Japan. Amazon will not act as importer for FBA shipments [s22][s23]. Since 1 October 2023, a person living abroad who clears customs must appoint an **Attorney for Customs Procedures (ACP)**, an agent with an address in Japan who handles the customs paperwork for you [s19][s20]. Japan also tightened who may count as the importer, so an agency that only handles paperwork cannot itself be the importer [s21]. Details are in the 'tax' and 'fulfil' sections.
**Consumption tax.** Your sales in Japan may be taxable. Whether you must register depends on your sales level and choices you make (see 'tax').
**Product-safety responsibility.** From 25 December 2025, overseas sellers of PSE/PSC products need a domestic administrator in Japan [s24].

blocks.p: Amazon.co.jp charges fees to your credit card and pays your proceeds to your bank account every two weeks [s1]. Overseas sellers can usually be paid to a supported foreign bank account through Amazon's currency converter for sellers or a third-party payment service. Check supported countries and the conversion fee in Seller Central first, because the conversion margin comes out of your profit.

callout.title: Do not guess the importer setup
callout.text: If your shipment arrives in Japan without a proper importer and ACP arrangement, it can be held at customs. Agree your IOR/ACP setup in writing before you book freight [s19][s22].

sections.title: Opening your Amazon.co.jp seller account step by step

head: Plan

rows: ¥100 per item sold, no monthly fee [s2]
Testing with a handful of sales. No advertising or promotions, bulk listing tools or most reports [s1][s2].
Anyone who plans to sell about 50 or more items a month (Amazon's own suggestion) [s2], run ads, register a brand or use Business features.
table.note: Referral fees and FBA fees are charged on top of the plan fee on both plans. You can switch plans later [s2].

blocks.p: Simple rule: if you will sell more than 49 units a month, the large-volume plan is cheaper (49 × ¥100 = ¥4,900). And because you cannot run Sponsored Products ads on the small-volume plan, almost every brand launch needs the large-volume plan [s2].
Amazon checks your identity and business before you can sell. Requirements change, so follow the list Seller Central shows you during sign-up. Typically you will be asked for:

ul: A valid passport or Japanese identity document (name must match exactly everywhere).
A credit card that can be charged internationally (for the plan fee).
A bank account for payouts (Japanese or a supported overseas account).
For companies: company registration documents. For Japanese companies this is usually the certificate of registered matters (登記簿謄本).
Proof of address, such as a recent bank or utility statement, if requested.
Your Japanese qualified invoice registration number (T + 13 digits), if you have one. It is optional at sign-up but needed if you want to issue qualified invoices (see 'tax').

blocks.p: Amazon may ask for a video call with your ID documents and may confirm your address by post or with a code. Make sure every name and address you enter matches your documents character for character (romanised names are a common source of mismatches).

For a well-prepared seller this usually takes from a few days to a few weeks. Delays almost always come from document mismatches or extra verification requests, so finish this before you order inventory.

blocks.h3: Common reasons for rejection or delay

ul: Name or address on the account does not match the ID or bank statement.
Blurry, cropped or expired documents.
Using a credit card or bank account in someone else's name.
Opening a second account, or using an address that does not match your documents.

sections.title: Every cost of selling on Amazon Japan

blocks.p: On Amazon Japan, **FBA fees are shown including 10% consumption tax**, while the **referral fee rates and the large-volume plan fee are before tax**, with 10% tax charged on top [s1]. Keep that in mind when you compare numbers, and confirm the exact fee for your product with the revenue calculator or fee preview in Seller Central.

A **referral fee** is Amazon's commission: a percentage of the total sale price (item price plus shipping and gift wrap), or a minimum of ¥30 per item, whichever is greater [s1]. Most categories charge 5% on items of ¥750 or less and a higher rate above that; since 1 April 2026 the higher rates are 0.4 points above their old level [s1][s3]. Amazon decides which fee category your product falls into, and METI has noted that the criteria are not always clear to sellers [s43].

sections.title: Tax and legal basics in Japan

callout.title: Not tax advice
callout.text: Japanese consumption tax and corporate tax rules are detailed and change with yearly tax reforms. Use this section to ask the right questions, then confirm with a Japanese tax accountant (税理士).

blocks.p: Japan's **consumption tax** is a VAT-style tax. The standard rate is **10%**, and a reduced **8%** rate applies to certain items such as most food and non-alcoholic drinks [s13]. Prices shown to Japanese consumers include tax.

**Who has to pay it?** In principle, a business (Japanese or foreign) is exempt if its taxable sales in the 'base period' (generally two years earlier) were **¥10 million or less** [s12]. New businesses can therefore often start without filing, but there are exceptions (for example for some newly formed companies), so confirm your status with the National Tax Agency or a tax accountant.

blocks.h3: The qualified invoice system (インボイス制度)

blocks.p: Since **1 October 2023**, businesses in Japan can generally only deduct the consumption tax they paid on purchases if they keep a **qualified invoice** from a registered issuer, with transitional relief for purchases from unregistered sellers [s13]. A registered issuer gets a registration number (the letter T plus 13 digits).

ul: **Registration is voluntary.** But once you register, you become a taxable business and must file consumption tax returns even if your sales are below ¥10 million [s12].

The transitional '20% special measure' for small businesses that registered covered taxation periods up to 30 September 2026 [s13]. The April 2026 amendment adds a follow-on measure for small sole proprietors [s46]; ask a tax accountant whether it applies to you.
Foreign businesses can apply using a dedicated application form for foreign businesses, submitted to the district tax office [s12].

**Why register?** Amazon Business buyers (companies) want qualified invoices so they can deduct the tax. If you cannot give one, business buyers may choose a registered competitor [s12]. If you only sell to consumers, registration matters less.
In Seller Central, you can enter your registration number in your tax settings so it appears on invoices Amazon generates. Check the current setting name in Seller Central.

blocks.h3: Who collects consumption tax on Amazon today?

blocks.p: For physical goods, **you do**, not Amazon (as of late 2026). Japan's existing platform taxation covers digital services sold by foreign businesses, not goods [s12]. The April 2026 amendment extends it to goods: from **1 April 2028**, platforms designated by the National Tax Agency (more than ¥5 billion a year of qualifying sales) must file and pay consumption tax on goods foreign sellers sell in Japan through them, and on low-value items (¥10,000 or less) shipped to Japanese buyers from abroad [s46]. Watch for Amazon's notices about how this will work in practice.

blocks.h3: Import consumption tax and the IOR

blocks.p: When goods enter Japan, the importer pays customs duty (if any) and **import consumption tax** at the time of import. Only the importer of record can normally claim that import tax back as a credit [s22][s23]. That is a key reason overseas sellers should import in their own name through an ACP instead of letting a forwarder act as importer [s22].

An individual without an address in Japan, or a company without an office in Japan, must appoint a **tax agent** (納税管理人) to handle tax returns, notifications and payment [s12]. Confirm filing deadlines with the National Tax Agency or your accountant.

If you live in Japan, profit from Amazon sales is taxable as business income (individual) or corporate income (company), and you file a return each year. If you are based abroad without a permanent establishment in Japan, your home country normally taxes your profit, but check your country's tax treaty with Japan. In both cases, keep Amazon's settlement reports, import papers and invoices for every shipment.

ul: Before you register for the qualified invoice system.
Before you import as a foreign business (IOR/ACP and import tax credits).
When your Japan sales approach ¥10 million a year [s12].
Before April 2028, to plan for platform taxation [s46].

sections.title: Product compliance, restrictions and brand protection

blocks.p: Japan has strict product-safety laws and regulators actively test products bought online. Amazon will remove non-compliant listings, and regulators can ask platforms to stop sales [s26][s27].

Some categories need Amazon's approval before you can list (for example certain food, beverages, cosmetics, medical devices, watches and some brands). Seller Central shows an 'apply to sell' button when a category is gated. Prescription drugs, many supplements claiming medical effects, weapons and counterfeit goods are prohibited.

blocks.h3: PSE: Electrical Appliances and Materials Safety Act (電気用品安全法)

ul: Most mains-powered electrical products, power adapters and mobile batteries need the **PSE** mark. Higher-risk 'specified' products need third-party conformity checks and carry a diamond-shaped PSE mark; others carry a round PSE mark. Check METI's product lists for yours.
The legal duty sits with the manufacturer or importer, who must notify METI and keep test records.
From **25 December 2025**, overseas businesses selling directly to Japanese consumers through platforms are clearly covered and must appoint a responsible person in Japan [s24][s25].

blocks.h3: PSC: Consumer Product Safety Act (消費生活用製品安全法)

blocks.p: A list of 'specified products' (for example certain helmets, pressure cookers, baby beds, lighters and laser pointers) need the **PSC** mark before sale. The same December 2025 amendment that covers PSE also covers PSC and adds the domestic-administrator duty for overseas sellers [s24]. Check METI's current list, because new product types (including some children's products) are being added.

blocks.h3: Radio Law (電波法): Giteki/TELEC for wireless products

ul: Anything that transmits radio signals (Bluetooth earphones, speakers, Wi-Fi devices, wireless chargers with radio functions, drones, keyless entry systems) generally needs **technical conformity certification** and the **Giteki mark** before it is sold or used in Japan [s28].
The mark can be small, but it must be easy to identify; devices with a screen may show it electronically [s28].

The Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (MIC) has a guideline for online shopping malls on non-compliant wireless devices [s26], runs test purchases and asks sellers to stop selling devices that fail [s27].
In your listing, include the certification number and show the mark in images.

blocks.p: Food, drinks, food additives, items that touch food (tableware, containers, cooking tools) and some toys for infants are covered. Importers generally must file an import notification with a quarantine station of the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW), and some materials need lab tests. A silicone spatula or a water bottle can count, so check with the MHLW quarantine station before you order.

Cosmetics and quasi-drugs are regulated under Japan's pharmaceutical law, and importing them generally requires a licensed marketing authorisation holder in Japan; check with MHLW or your prefectural government before you import. Medical or health claims ('cures', 'treats') are not allowed for ordinary products and will get listings removed.

ul: Labels, warnings and instructions should be in **Japanese**. Electrical, food and cosmetic products have specific label content rules.
Your listing title, bullets and description should be written in natural Japanese. Machine-translated text lowers conversion and can make safety information unclear.

blocks.h3: Act on Specified Commercial Transactions (特定商取引法)

blocks.p: This law requires online sellers to show key information to buyers, such as the seller's name, address, phone number, price, payment and delivery terms, and return policy. On Amazon much of this appears on your seller profile, so keep it accurate and complete. Check the Consumer Affairs Agency's guidance for the full list.

ul: **Brand Registry** gives you control of your brand's listings, A+ content, Brand Store, Sponsored Brands ads and brand-protection tools. It needs a registered or pending trademark from an eligible office; for Japan that is the **Japan Patent Office (JPO)**.
JPO examination usually takes many months. Check the JPO's current waiting times and fast-track (accelerated examination) options before you plan your launch.

**IP Accelerator** is Amazon's program that connects brands with IP law firms at pre-negotiated fees, and can give earlier access to Brand Registry tools while a trademark is pending. Check in Brand Registry whether it currently covers Japan.
Consider registering your brand in katakana as well as Latin letters if shoppers will search for it that way.

callout.title: Overseas sellers of electrical or wireless goods
callout.text: Since 25 December 2025 you need a Japanese domestic administrator for PSE/PSC products [s24], and wireless products need Giteki certification [s28]. Missing either can lead to listing removal and regulator action.

sections.title: Choosing your first product with data

ul: Sells for about **¥2,000–¥6,000**. Below about ¥1,000, fixed fees eat your margin (see Example B: Amazon takes about 34%) [s1].
Fits in the **small or standard** FBA tiers and weighs under 1 kg.
Not electrical, wireless, food-contact, cosmetic or for babies, so no PSE, Giteki or Food Sanitation Act paperwork on your first product [s24][s28].
Not seasonal (or you launch well before the season).
Can be improved in a way reviewers care about (sizing that fits Japanese homes, quieter, better instructions in Japanese, better packaging).
Top listings have few reviews, or reviews complain about the same fixable problem.

blocks.p: Aim for Amazon fees plus landed cost to be **no more than about 60% of your selling price**, leaving room for ads, consumption tax and profit. Using Example A (a ¥3,000 home and kitchen item): Amazon fees are about ¥826 [s1]. If your landed cost (product + freight + duty) is ¥900, that is ¥1,726, or 58% of price. If you are a registered taxable business, about ¥273 of the price is consumption tax (less input tax credits) [s13]. That leaves roughly ¥1,000 before ads and storage. If you spend ¥450 on ads per sale at launch, you still keep about ¥550 (18%). That is a workable example; anything much thinner is risky.

blocks.h3: Validate demand with Amazon's own tools

ol: **Product Opportunity Explorer** (in Seller Central, if available on your account): see search volume and click share for niches in Japan.
**Search Amazon.co.jp in Japanese**: check the first page for the main keyword, count reviews, look at prices and read 1–3 star reviews for problems you can solve.
**Revenue Calculator / fee preview**: enter dimensions and price to see exact referral and FBA fees.
**Brand Analytics** (after Brand Registry): see top search terms and what shoppers click.
**Amazon Ads console keyword suggestions**: see suggested bids, which tell you how competitive a keyword is.

ul: **Electrical or wireless** without a certification plan [s24][s28].
**Seasonal** items you cannot launch at least two months before demand starts (for example winter heating goods, summer cooling goods).
**Gated** categories you are not approved for.
**Patented or trademarked designs**: search the JPO database (J-PlatPat) before ordering.
**Heavy or oversized** items: large tiers cost far more to fulfil (from ¥589 per unit) [s1].
**Long-tail stock risk**: anything you might hold more than 365 days pays a long-term storage fee [s1].

sections.title: FBA, FBM and getting stock into Japan

head: Option
What it is
Good for
rows: Amazon stores, ships and handles returns and customer service for orders. Items become Prime-eligible.
Most beginners. Fast delivery wins the Buy Box and conversion.
You store and ship orders yourself or through a Japanese logistics company.
Large or slow items, very low volumes, or sellers in Japan with their own warehouse.
Seller-fulfilled Prime (マケプレプライム)
You ship yourself but meet Amazon's speed and quality standards to show the Prime badge.
Experienced sellers with strong Japanese logistics. Check current eligibility and standards in Seller Central.

blocks.p: The **Buy Box** is the 'Add to cart' button on a product page. When several sellers offer the same item, Amazon chooses one to get the Buy Box based on price, delivery speed and seller performance. FBA usually helps because of fast, reliable delivery.

ol: **Set up the importer**: you (as importer of record, with an ACP appointed) or a Japanese IOR service or distributor [s19][s22]. Amazon does not act as importer [s22][s23].
**Book freight**: air for first small batches, sea for later volume. Use a forwarder experienced with Amazon Japan FBA deliveries.
**Customs clearance**: your customs broker files the import declaration; duty and import consumption tax are paid at import [s22].

**Delivery to Amazon**: create a shipment plan in Seller Central, follow Amazon Japan's delivery appointment and packaging rules, and use the labels Amazon gives you. Keep PSE/Giteki/food papers ready in case customs or Amazon asks.

ul: Every unit needs a scannable barcode: either the manufacturer barcode (JAN/EAN) if allowed, or an Amazon product label.
Put a Japanese label on each product with your company name and required warnings, and use outer cartons that protect the retail box.
Aim to hold roughly **4–8 weeks** of stock in FBA. Holding far more (reported as over 26 weeks of cover) triggers the storage surcharge [s5].
Peak storage (October–December) costs about 1.8 times the normal rate [s1], so time big shipments for just before Black Friday, not in early autumn.
Remove or liquidate stock that will sit more than a year, because of the long-term storage fee after 365 days [s1].

sections.title: Your first 90 days, week by week

blocks.h3: Weeks 1–2: build a listing that converts

ul: **Title** in Japanese: brand + what it is + key feature + size/quantity.
**Five bullet points** answering the real questions Japanese shoppers ask (size in cm, materials, how to clean, what's in the box, warranty).
**Images**: 7+ images, white background for the main image, lifestyle shots in Japanese-style homes, an infographic with Japanese text, and a size comparison.
**A+ content** (after Brand Registry): comparison charts and brand story with Japanese text.
**Price**: set a launch price you can sustain.

blocks.h3: Weeks 3–4: first sales and first reviews

ul: Enrol in **Amazon Vine** if you have Brand Registry and the product qualifies; Vine reviewers get free units and write honest reviews. Check the current Vine fee in Seller Central.
Start **Sponsored Products** automatic and manual campaigns (see 'ads').
Use a small **coupon** (for example 5–10% off) to improve click-through.
Reply to every customer message in Japanese within 24 hours. Amazon tracks response time.

blocks.p: **What 'good' looks like at day 30:** listing indexed for your main keywords, first 5–10 reviews (Vine plus organic), ads spending to plan, no account-health warnings.

ul: Read the search term report weekly; move converting search terms into exact-match campaigns and add negatives for irrelevant ones.
Use **Request a Review** in Seller Central for orders 5–30 days old.
Check your inventory: reorder in time to avoid stock-outs, which kill ranking.

blocks.p: **What 'good' looks like at day 60:** steady daily sales, conversion rate stable or rising, ad cost per sale falling, 15+ reviews with 4 stars or more.

ul: Increase bids on profitable keywords and add Sponsored Brands (Brand Registry needed).
Plan for the next big event (see 'grow'): submit deals early, because Amazon closes submissions weeks before events.
Build a simple Brand Store.

blocks.p: **What 'good' looks like at day 90:** you know your true profit per unit after ads, a growing share of sales from organic (non-ad) search, and a reorder already on the way.

ol: **Auto campaign**: let Amazon find search terms. Low bids, all match groups on.
**Manual broad/phrase campaign**: 10–20 Japanese keywords from your research, including hiragana and katakana variants.
**Manual exact campaign**: your 3–5 best keywords, added as you find winners.
**Product targeting campaign**: target competitor products where you have a better price, rating or feature.

blocks.p: Many beginners start with about ¥1,000–¥2,000 a day in total across campaigns for one product (an example, not an Amazon figure). Start with Amazon's suggested bid in the Ads console, because Amazon does not publish average cost-per-click figures for Japan.

ul: **ACoS (advertising cost of sales)** = ad spend ÷ ad sales. If you spend ¥10,000 and get ¥40,000 in ad sales, ACoS is 25%.
**TACoS (total ACoS)** = ad spend ÷ total sales (ad + organic). It shows whether ads are building organic sales over time.
**Break-even ACoS** = your profit margin before ads. In Example A above, profit before ads is about ¥1,000 on ¥3,000 (33%), so ACoS above 33% loses money on each ad sale.
During launch, ACoS above break-even is normal for a few weeks. After day 60, aim for ACoS below break-even and a falling TACoS.

blocks.p: A **negative keyword** stops your ad showing for a search. Add negatives for irrelevant searches (wrong product type, 'used' (中古), 'free') and check the search term report every week.

ol: Download the search term report.
Add converting search terms to exact match; add negatives for terms with clicks and no sales.
Lower bids on keywords far above break-even ACoS; raise bids slightly on profitable ones.
Check budget: if a profitable campaign runs out of budget early in the day, increase it.

ul: Use **Amazon Vine** for early reviews (Brand Registry needed).

Use the **Request a Review** button or Amazon's automated review requests. Do not ask for positive reviews, and do not offer refunds, gifts or discounts for reviews; this is against Amazon policy and can get your account suspended.
Fix the problem behind negative reviews (product, instructions, packaging), then update the listing.

blocks.p: Once you have Brand Registry, build a **Brand Store** (your mini-website on Amazon), use A+ content, and check Brand Analytics for search terms. These need a JPO trademark (registered or pending, depending on program rules).
Japan has a busy Amazon event calendar. Submit deals well ahead; Amazon closes deal submission weeks before each event.

sections.title: Common beginner mistakes and account-health risks

ol: **Selling electrical or wireless goods without PSE or Giteki.** Listings get removed, and regulators run test purchases [s24][s27]. Get certification first.
**No domestic administrator (overseas sellers).** Required for PSE/PSC products since 25 December 2025 [s24].
**Shipping to Japan without an importer of record and ACP.** Goods can be stuck at customs; Amazon will not be your importer [s19][s22].
**Machine-translated Japanese.** Lowers conversion and trust. Pay a native writer.
**Using 2025 fee tables.** Referral fees rose 0.4 points on most items over ¥750 from April 2026 [s3].
**Pricing just under ¥1,000 without checking fees.** Fixed FBA fees take a large share of cheap items [s1].
**Sending too much stock.** Too many weeks of cover triggers a surcharge [s5]; over 365 days triggers the long-term storage fee [s1].
**Ignoring consumption tax.** Forgetting that Japanese prices include tax, or registering for the invoice system without understanding the filing duty [s12].
**Review manipulation.** Paying for reviews, review swaps, or 'refund after review' schemes lead to suspension. Use Vine and Request a Review only.
**IP complaints.** Copying a brand's images, using a trademarked name in your title, or selling a patented design. Search J-PlatPat first.
**Slow customer replies.** Reply within 24 hours, in Japanese, every day including weekends.
**Medical or exaggerated claims.** Claims like 'cures' or 'prevents disease' break Japanese law and Amazon policy.

Run the margin example: fees + landed cost under about 60% of price.
File a JPO trademark (consider IP Accelerator).

Overseas sellers of PSE/PSC products: appoint a domestic administrator [s24].
Talk to a Japanese tax accountant about consumption tax and the qualified invoice system [s12][s13].
Collect ID, company and bank documents with matching names.
Register on the large-volume plan (¥4,900/month before tax) [s1].
Complete identity verification.
Order samples; pick a supplier; order a first batch of about 6–8 weeks of expected sales.
Prepare Japanese labels, barcodes and protective cartons.
Book freight and customs clearance; create the FBA shipment plan.
Write the listing with a native Japanese writer; shoot 7+ images.
Apply for Brand Registry when your trademark is filed.
Enrol in Vine and add A+ content after Brand Registry.
Launch Sponsored Products (auto + manual) with a fixed daily budget.
Reply to every message within 24 hours.
Review search terms and bids weekly.
Reorder before stock runs low; avoid more than 26 weeks of cover [s5].
Plan deals for the next event (Black Friday, Hatsuuri, Prime Day) [s33][s34][s35].
Watch for the 2028 platform-taxation changes and Amazon notices in 2027 [s46].

faq.q: Can I sell on Amazon Japan if I don't live in Japan?
faq.a: Yes. Overseas individuals and companies can register on Amazon.co.jp. The hard parts are importing (Amazon won't be your importer, so you need your own importer of record and a customs agent in Japan), consumption tax, and appointing a person in Japan for electrical and other regulated products since December 2025.

faq.q: Which seller plan should I choose, small-volume or large-volume?
faq.a: The large-volume plan costs ¥4,900 a month before tax; the small-volume plan costs ¥100 per item sold. If you'll sell 50 or more items a month, or want to run ads or register a brand, choose large-volume.

faq.q: How much does Amazon take per sale in Japan?
faq.a: It depends on category, price and size. As an example, a ¥3,000 home and kitchen item in the Standard 1 FBA tier pays a ¥462 referral fee (15.4%, with 10% consumption tax added on the fee) plus a ¥318 FBA fee, around 28% of the price. Cheap items under ¥1,000 often lose 30% or more to fees.

faq.q: Did Amazon Japan raise fees in 2026?
faq.a: Yes. From 1 April 2026, referral fees rose 0.4 percentage points on items selling for more than ¥750, while Amazon said FBA fees for standard items measuring 20–80 cm and up to 5 kg fell by an average of ¥38. Stock held more than 365 days also pays a long-term storage fee; check the current rate in Seller Central.

faq.q: Do I need to register for the invoice system (インボイス) to sell on Amazon?
faq.a: No, it's voluntary, and you can still sell without it. Register if you want to sell to businesses (they need qualified invoices to deduct tax), but remember that once registered you must file consumption tax returns even if your sales are below ¥10 million.

faq.q: Does Amazon collect consumption tax for me?
faq.a: Not for physical goods as of late 2026; the seller is responsible. Under the April 2026 Consumption Tax Act amendment, designated large platforms become liable for consumption tax on goods sold by foreign sellers from 1 April 2028, so this will change for many overseas sellers.

faq.q: Can Amazon be my importer of record for FBA in Japan?
faq.a: No. Amazon does not act as importer of record for FBA shipments. Non-residents importing in their own name must appoint an Attorney for Customs Procedures (ACP) in Japan, or use a Japanese importer or distributor.

faq.q: Do I need PSE for a USB charger or power bank?
faq.a: Generally yes. Most mains-powered electrical products, adapters and mobile batteries need PSE marking under Japan's electrical safety law. Check METI's lists to see whether your product needs third-party testing (diamond PSE) or self-declaration (round PSE).

faq.q: My Bluetooth product has FCC and CE. Is that enough for Japan?
faq.a: No. Wireless products need Japanese technical conformity certification and the Giteki mark. The government runs test purchases from online stores and asks sellers to stop selling non-compliant devices.

faq.q: Can I write my listing in English?
faq.a: You can technically list with English text, but Japanese shoppers search and buy in Japanese. Listings written by a native Japanese speaker convert far better and are easier for Amazon's AI shopping assistant to understand.

faq.q: When are the big Amazon Japan sales?
faq.a: In 2026: New Year sale (Hatsuuri) 3–7 January, Smile Sales in several months, Prime Day 10–13 July, the autumn Prime sale 16–19 October and Black Friday from 27 November to 7 December. Submit deals weeks in advance.

Yes. Rufus opened to all customers in Japan in September 2025 and was renamed 'Alexa for Shopping' in November 2026. It answers shopper questions using your listing, images and reviews, so clear Japanese content matters.

faq.q: How long does a Japanese trademark take, and do I need one for Brand Registry?
faq.a: You need a JPO trademark (registered, or pending through programs like IP Accelerator) for Brand Registry in Japan. JPO examination usually takes many months; check the JPO's current average waiting time and consider fast-track options.

faq.q: What gets Amazon Japan accounts suspended most often?
faq.a: Review manipulation, selling uncertified electrical or wireless products, IP complaints, inauthentic item complaints without supplier invoices, and opening multiple accounts. High late-shipment or cancellation rates on self-fulfilled orders also hurt account health.
